title: Market Research Exclusions - Canadian SR&ED Tax Glossary
description: Learn why Market Research and sales promotion are ineligible for Canadian R&D tax credits in our comprehensive SR&ED glossary.
summary: Under Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program, market research activities such as market validation and commercialization planning fall outside eligible R&D. For Canadian businesses claiming federal investment tax credits under the Income Tax Act, commercial market risk does not establish technological uncertainty; only systematic investigation resolving scientific or technological uncertainty qualifies.

body.text: Under Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program, market research activities such as market validation and commercialization planning fall outside eligible R&D. For Canadian businesses claiming federal investment tax credits under the Income Tax Act, commercial market risk does not establish technological uncertainty; only systematic investigation resolving scientific or technological uncertainty qualifies.

Canada's flagship federal R&D tax incentive—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Program, governed primarily by subsection 248(1), section 37, section 127, and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act together with subsections 2900(4), 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9) and paragraph 2902(b) of the Income Tax Regulations—underwent its largest statutory expansion in over a decade when Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3) received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) doubled from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual refundable federal credit on current expenditures from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range widened from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million alongside a new elective three-year average gross revenue phase-out method, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) gained access to the 35% enhanced credit for the first time, and capital expenditures (together with Shared-Use-Equipment incentives) returned to the program for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, carrying 40% refundability on enhanced capital ITCs.

Three further 2026 developments reshape R&D compliance, administration, and provincial stacking across Canada. First, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process through My Business Account for eligible businesses with gross business income under $25 million, providing upfront technical eligibility decisions within eight weeks and cutting post-filing expenditure review targets from 180 days to 90 days. Second, Federal Budget 2026 ("Masters of our Destiny"), tabled on November 5, 2026, proposed expanding SR&ED for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, to cover initial regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs tied to eligible SR&ED projects, while again omitting a federal Patent Box regime. Third, provincial R&D regimes have diverged markedly: Québec replaced eight legacy R&D tax credits with its refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (30% on the first $1 million above an exclusion floor and 20% thereafter) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, whereas Ontario and Alberta retained legacy statutory caps ($3 million for the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit) and legacy taxable capital phase-out ranges ($10 million–$50 million for Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant) that did not expand alongside federal Bill C-15.
1. Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution (2024–2026)
1.1 Core Provisions of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

Canada's federal SR&ED tax incentive operates as a two-part statutory regime under the Income Tax Act (ITA) and Income Tax Regulations (ITR), pairing full deductibility of allowable R&D expenditures against business income with a volume-based Investment Tax Credit (ITC) that offsets Part I federal corporate or personal income tax payable or generates a direct cash refund. Audit verification of any Canadian R&D tax position turns on six interlocking groups of statutory and regulatory provisions.

First, subsection 248(1) of the ITA establishes the foundational legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" as systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Subsection 248(1) also contains the statutory definition of a corporation's "balance-due day" (specifically subparagraph (d)(i)), which interacts with refundable credit rules across corporate reorganizations.

Second, section 37 of the ITA governs the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada. Within section 37, subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) covers allowable current expenditures for SR&ED directly undertaken by the taxpayer; subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) through (iii) cover eligible contract expenditures performed on behalf of the taxpayer and third-party payments; paragraph 37(1)(b) (restored by Bill C-15 for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024) covers allowable SR&ED capital expenditures; paragraph 37(1)(f.1) addresses specific pool balance determinations; and subsection 37(11) establishes the strict 18-month prescribed form filing deadline.

Third, section 127 of the ITA houses the core calculation, limitation, timing, and recapture mechanics for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits. Subsection 127(5) authorizes the deduction of ITCs against Part I tax otherwise payable, including carryback and carryforward rules. Subsection 127(9) sets out the central statutory definitions—most notably "investment tax credit" (including paragraph (m), which bars ITC claims if prescribed forms are not filed within 18 months of tax year-end), "qualified expenditure" (including the 80% inclusion rule for arm's-length SR&ED contracts and third-party payments, Shared-Use-Equipment inclusions under paragraph 127(9)(c), and exclusions), "contract payment", "first term shared-use-equipment", and "second term shared-use-equipment". Subsections 127(10.2), 127(10.3), and 127(10.5) govern the annual expenditure limit for CCPCs, mandatory allocation of that limit among associated corporations, and proration across multiple or short taxation years. Subsection 127(11.2) sets out the time-of-acquisition ("available for use") rule when applying subsections 127(5), 127(7), and 127(8). Subsection 127(25) addresses deemed contract payments; subsection 127(26) (cross-referenced in subsection 127(11.6)) deems current expenditures unpaid 180 days after tax year-end not to have been incurred until paid; and subsections 127(27), 127(28), 127(29), and 127(32) impose ITC recapture on disposed or converted SR&ED property, partnership property, and allocated property.

Fourth, section 127.1 of the ITA governs the refundable investment tax credit, with subsection 127.1(2) defining "qualifying corporation" for cash refund entitlement. Fifth, general corporate, property, partnership, and tax-exempt provisions interact directly with SR&ED claims: paragraph 20(1)(a) and subsection 13(21) link SR&ED capital property eligibility to depreciable property and undepreciated capital cost (UCC) under Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules; paragraphs 87(2)(l), 87(2)(l.1), 87(2)(l.2), and 87(2)(oo.1) preserve section 37 pools, section 37.1, Part VIII history, and subsection 127.1(2) qualifying corporation status upon corporate amalgamations; subsection 96(1) (together with subsection 1102(1a) of the ITR) requires partnership property and SR&ED income calculations to be accounted for at the partnership level; subsection 125(7) defines "Canadian-controlled private corporation" (CCPC); and section 149 identifies tax-exempt public authorities and entities whose R&D funding constitutes a contract payment reducing qualified expenditures.

Sixth, the Income Tax Regulations define notional overhead and prescribed exclusions: subsection 2900(4) sets the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on the eligible salary base, subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) cap specified employee proxy salaries, subsection 2900(9) lists salary base exclusions, and paragraph 2902(b) defines prescribed current and capital expenditures (such as used equipment, interest and financing charges, and scientific society membership dues) barred from earning ITCs.
1.2 Chronology of Enacted Reforms: From the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15

Between late 2024 and late 2026, federal SR&ED policy evolved across four distinct legislative and administrative milestones. Distinguishing early consultation proposals from enacted law is essential during tax audits because outdated transitional figures remain widespread in secondary online commentary.

On December 16, 2024, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed increasing the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, widening the taxable capital phase-out range, extending the enhanced credit rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring capital expenditure eligibility. On August 15, 2025, the Department of Finance released draft legislative proposals (with public consultation closing September 12, 2025) detailing technical mechanics, including 40% partial refundability on enhanced capital ITCs. Then, on November 4, 2025, Federal Budget 2025 superseded the earlier $4.5 million figure by doubling the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3 million directly to $6 million. Finally, on March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, enacting the $6 million expenditure limit, the $15 million–$75 million phase-out range, the elective three-year gross revenue test, ECPC access, and restored capital and Shared-Use-Equipment eligibility into binding federal law. Between April 1, 2026, and October 7, 2026, the CRA launched its Pre-Claim Approval portal and published updated versions of Form T661, T2 Schedules 31 and 49, Forms T1145 and T1146, and five core SR&ED administrative policies.

A critical technical audit point under Bill C-15 is that its effective dates are bifurcated. The $6 million expenditure limit, the $15 million–$75 million phase-out thresholds, the three-year gross revenue election, and ECPC eligibility apply based on when the taxation year begins—specifically to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, beginning on or after December 16, 2024; for a calendar-year corporation, the 2025 tax year beginning January 1, 2025, is the first qualifying year). Conversely, the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures and lease outlays applies on a property-acquisition and lease-incurrence basis to depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, and equipment lease costs incurred/first payable after December 15, 2024—even if the claimant's taxation year began prior to December 16, 2024 (in which case SR&ED operating-time percentages are measured across operating time after December 15, 2024). Specialist tax advisors at Scitax Advisory Partners have also noted a technical statutory interaction with subsection 127(11.2) as amended by Bill C-15: because subsection 127(11.2) governs the "time of acquisition" (tying acquisition to when property becomes available for use) when applying subsections 127(5), 127(7), and 127(8), capital equipment purchased prior to December 16, 2024, that first became available for use after December 15, 2024, presents distinct timing rules for ITC claims versus section 37 expense deductibility.
During compliance verification, auditors must correct four recurring errors found in legacy tax guides and older blog articles:

items: Enhanced Expenditure Limit ($6 Million, Not $3 Million or $4.5 Million): Some secondary legal commentary continued to cite the superseded $4.5 million 2024 Fall Economic Statement proposal or the pre-2025 $3 million cap. Under enacted Bill C-15 and CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), the statutory limit for tax years starting after December 15, 2024, is $6,000,000.

Prescribed Proxy Amount Rate (55%, Not 65%): Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the Prescribed Proxy Amount rate was reduced from 65% in 2012 to 60% in 2013, and has stood at 55% of the salary base since 2014. Using 65% overstates proxy overhead by ten percentage points.

Eligible Public Corporations Now Qualify: The historical rule restricting the enhanced 35% credit solely to CCPCs ended for tax years beginning after December 15, 2024; qualifying ECPCs now earn the 35% rate up to $6 million.

Capital Equipment Eligibility Restored: The Budget 2012 repeal of capital expenditures (effective since 2014) has been reversed for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024.

body.text: 1.3 Federal Budget 2026 Proposals and Omission of the Federal Patent Box

On November 5, 2026, the federal government tabled Budget 2026, titled "Masters of our Destiny". In Chapter 1 (Boosting Innovation and Commercialisation) and Tax Measures: Supplementary Information (pages 117 and 402–403), Budget 2026 proposed expanding the front-end SR&ED program to include targeted downstream commercialization and IP protection expenditures, projected by the Department of Finance to deliver $930 million over five years and $235 million per year ongoing. As proposed, these changes apply to taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day (November 5, 2026)—meaning a corporation with a December 31 year-end would first benefit in its taxation year starting January 1, 2027, contingent upon legislative enactment. Claiming these commercialization outlays prior to Royal Assent of the implementing bill invites reassessment.

The Budget 2026 SR&ED proposal operates within the existing 35% enhanced and 15% basic SR&ED rate structure (though practitioner analyses note the budget text leaves certain granular rate and administrative mechanics to draft legislation and forthcoming CRA sector-specific commercialization guidance). Both proposed expenditure streams require a direct nexus to an underlying project that qualifies under existing SR&ED eligibility rules:

items: Initial Regulatory Approval and Certification Testing: Adds tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process. Eligible cost categories mirror standard SR&ED rules (salaries and wages, materials, subcontractor payments, overhead, and machinery and equipment). Routine quality control, routine testing excluded under existing SR&ED rules, post-approval testing to keep a product on the market, and unmentioned licence renewals or recertifications do not qualify.

Registration and Maintenance of SR&ED-Developed Intellectual Property: Adds costs reasonably incurred to register and maintain IP protection—covering patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software—where the IP was developed in the course of conducting an eligible SR&ED project. Qualifying outlays include preparing and filing patent applications and periodic maintenance fees (with advisors cautioning claimants to review with patent agents where application preparation work is physically performed relative to foreign office fees). IP enforcement costs such as infringement litigation are expressly excluded, and if the taxpayer subsequently disposes of the IP (including in a corporate asset or business sale), recapture rules will apply to claw back the related SR&ED deduction and ITC.

body.text: In contrast to this front-end SR&ED expansion, both Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025) and Budget 2026 (November 5, 2026) omitted a federal Patent Box (IP Box) tax regime. Although promised in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and the April 2025 federal election platform as a preferential tax rate on income derived from commercializing IP retained in Canada, legislative tracking confirms that as of November 2026 no bill in the 45th Parliament, Notice of Ways and Means Motion, Canada Gazette Part II regulation, or CRA tax schedule exists for a Patent Box. Tax teams must not confuse a Patent Box with the Productivity Mega Deduction announced on September 15, 2026 (with draft legislation released October 1, 2026, and extended in Budget 2026 to raise the deduction rate for Canadian development expense from 30% to 100%), which is an immediate-expensing Capital Cost Allowance measure rather than an IP income tax regime. Instead, federal IP support outside SR&ED relies on direct Budget 2025 appropriations: $84.4 million over four years (starting in 2026–2027) to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) to extend Elevate IP, $75 million for the National Research Council (NRC) IP Assist Program, and $22.5 million for the Patent Collective. Budget 2026 also introduced broader corporate tax reforms relevant to innovative companies, including creating the Canada Growth Incentive (extending entrepreneurial capital-gains rollover reinvestment windows by three years for dispositions on or after January 1, 2027), consulting on intra-provincial corporate loss transfers, extending the Clean Electricity and Clean Technology ITCs to 2040 (from 2034) and the 15% Mineral Exploration Tax Credit / 30% Critical Mineral Exploration Tax Credit to March 31, 2032, and exempting CCPCs from the Part VI.1 taxable preferred share regime on dividends paid on or after November 5, 2026 (while raising the dividend allowance for non-CCPCs from $500,000 to $1,500,000 and the reduction threshold from $1,000,000 to $3,000,000 for tax years ending after 2026).

body.text: 1.4 Macro Program Scale and Sectoral Distribution

Official CRA program statistics confirm rapid expansion in SR&ED participation and fiscal outlay. In fiscal year 2024–2025, the SR&ED program delivered $4.5 billion in investment tax credits across more than 19,000 claimants and more than 22,000 processed claims. (One accounting firm guide cites more than 24,160 businesses annually, whereas Government of Canada figures for FY 2024–2025 report 19,000+ claimants and 22,000+ claims.) For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026 (FY 2025–2026), CRA annual statistics show $4.9 billion in ITCs claimed and $4.6 billion allowed—a cumulative increase of roughly 50% in allowed credit value since fiscal year 2022.

Of the $4.6 billion in credits allowed in FY 2025–2026, 59% were refundable and 41% were non-refundable. By technical field, software development accounted for 42.6% of all ITCs allowed in FY 2025–2026, rising from 35.7% in FY 2021–2022. By firm size (measured by gross income), smaller businesses under $4 million filed 65% of all claims and earned 33% of allowed credit dollars, mid-sized enterprises ($4 million to $20 million and $20 million to $250 million) earned 23% and 22% respectively, and large enterprises exceeding $250 million filed 3% of claims while capturing 22% of total credit value. Historical CRA jurisdictional data (Table 4B for the 2021 tax year, totalling $3,845.1 million across corporations at an average claim of $162,200) further illustrates the geographic breadth of claims, led by multi-jurisdiction corporations operating across multiple provinces ($1,482.8 million across 1,660 corporations, averaging roughly $893,000 each), alongside regional cohorts in Ontario, Québec, British Columbia, Alberta, Nova Scotia ($22.0 million across 260 corporations), Saskatchewan ($20.6 million across 3,190 corporations), New Brunswick ($14.6 million across 190 corporations), Newfoundland and Labrador ($7.5 million across 70 corporations), and Prince Edward Island ($2.3 million across 70 corporations).

body.text: 2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Framework
2.1 Categories of Eligible Work Under Subsection 248(1)

Any business carrying on R&D in Canada—across software and SaaS, artificial intelligence and machine learning, clean technology, biotechnology and life sciences, robotics, advanced manufacturing, agriculture, food and beverage, aerospace, and energy and resources—may submit an SR&ED claim regardless of company size or revenue stage. Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (mirrored in harmonized provincial definitions), eligible R&D requires rigorously organized systematic scientific or technical work carried out by experiment or analysis across three primary categories:

items: Basic Research: Systematic work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with no specific practical application in view.
Applied Research: Systematic work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Experimental Development: Systematic work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement to create new materials, products, devices, or processes, or to improve existing ones, explicitly including incremental improvements. In software and AI engineering, common qualifying territory includes backend system architecture, machine-learning model development, real-time processing systems, and novel algorithm design.

body.text: 2.2 The Three-Criterion CRA Eligibility Standard

While older practitioner guides sometimes break eligibility into a five-question checklist, modern CRA technical review practice and Form T661 project narratives evaluate every claimed project against three core mandatory criteria:

items: Scientific or Technological Uncertainty: The project must confront genuine technical challenges, system constraints, or limitations that cannot be resolved using standard engineering practice or publicly available knowledge. Routine product updates, commercial market risk, or routine software configuration do not establish technological uncertainty.

Scientific or Technological Advancement: The work must aim to generate new scientific knowledge or advance technological capability and understanding beyond the existing baseline. Even if a prototype or algorithm ultimately falls short of commercial deployment targets, systematic proof of why a technical path fails under given constraints still advances technological knowledge.

Systematic Investigation or Search: Overcoming the technological uncertainty must follow a structured, iterative experimental or analytical process—formulating hypotheses, executing controlled tests or analyses, evaluating empirical outcomes, and recording those steps in contemporaneous documentation created naturally during the R&D rather than reconstructed after year-end.

body.text: 2.3 Excluded Activities and Production-Run Boundaries

Not every technical or product-development expense qualifies as SR&ED. Existing statutory exclusions bar quality control and routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes, post-approval market-maintenance testing, and offshore R&D work performed outside Canada (subject only to narrow permissible-foreign-salary rules). Historically—and continuing for all taxation years beginning before November 5, 2026—downstream outlays for patent protection, regulatory approvals, market validation, product certification, and commercialization planning have also fallen outside federal SR&ED.

Where experimental development intersects with physical manufacturing or custom asset construction, CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy, and Materials for SR&ED Policy enforce strict perimeter rules. Any output beyond what is strictly required to conduct the experimental evaluation is classified as excess production and is ineligible. Furthermore, where materials or components claimed for SR&ED are incorporated into a custom product, commercial asset, experimental production run, or commercial production with experimental development that is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, SR&ED ITC recapture applies under subsection 127(27).
3. Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryover Rules
3.1 Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) Credit Rates
Under CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), federal SR&ED ITCs are calculated at two volume-based rates:

items: Enhanced ITC Rate (35%): Comprising the 15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement, earned by qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) and—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit.

Basic ITC Rate (15%): Earned by all other corporations (such as foreign-controlled corporations and non-qualifying public corporations), individuals (sole proprietorships), beneficiaries of trusts, members of partnerships, and CCPCs or ECPCs on qualified expenditures exceeding their annual expenditure limit. There is no statutory ceiling on the total volume of qualified R&D expenditures eligible for the 15% basic rate.

body.text: 3.2 The $6 Million Expenditure Limit, Phase-Out Tracks, and Associated Corporations

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the baseline annual expenditure limit for CCPCs and ECPCs doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, raising the maximum annual enhanced ITC from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Access to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out gradually under two statutory measurement tracks.

Under the default CCPC Taxable Capital Track (subsection 127(10.2)), a CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease once its (and its associated corporations') taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated (nil) once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000 (widened from the pre-Bill C-15 range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000). Across that $60,000,000 phase-out span, an illustrative linear reduction reduces the $6,000,000 limit by $1 for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000.

Under the Three-Year Average Annual Gross Revenue Track (introduced by Bill C-15), ECPCs—defined as corporations resident in Canada that are public corporations (including by reason of a listing on a designated stock exchange in Canada or abroad, such as the TSX, NYSE, or NASDAQ) and are not controlled, directly or indirectly, by one or more non-resident persons—must determine their expenditure limit reduction using the average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years. Per CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, this calculation aggregates average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of every corporation that is a member of the associated group for the taxation year in question over the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether those corporations were associated throughout that entire three-year period. Practitioner tax guides report the gross-revenue phase-out window across the same $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 band. Crucially, CCPCs may also elect (using the prescribed form) to compute their expenditure limit phase-out under this three-year average gross revenue method rather than taxable capital—preventing venture-backed biotech, cleantech, and deep-tech startups with over $15 million in balance-sheet equity/debt capital but low early-stage revenue from prematurely losing the 35% refundable credit.

Where two or more CCPCs are associated, they share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit and must file an allocation agreement under subsection 127(10.3) using T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated May 29, 2026). If a corporation has a short taxation year of less than 51 weeks, or if an associated CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year under subsection 127(10.5), its expenditure limit is prorated by the number of days in that taxation year divided by 365 (for example, 184 ÷ 365 for a July 1 to December 31 stub period).
3.3 Entity-Specific Refundability Matrix (Current vs. Capital Expenditures)

Whether unused SR&ED ITCs (after reducing Part I federal tax otherwise payable to nil) are refunded in cash under section 127.1 depends on both the claimant's legal entity category and whether the expenditure is current or capital. Under Bill C-15 and CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), enhanced 35% ITCs earned on current expenditures are 100% refundable (a 35.0% cash refund), whereas enhanced 35% ITCs earned on post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures are partially refundable at 40% (yielding a 35% × 40% = 14.0% immediate cash refund plus a 21.0% non-refundable ITC balance).

CRA policy further differentiates three classes of CCPCs—(1) a Qualifying Corporation (under subsection 127.1(2)) that is not an "excluded corporation", (2) an Excluded Corporation, and (3) a CCPC that is other than a qualifying or excluded corporation—alongside ECPCs, other corporations, unincorporated individuals/trusts, and partnership members. Notably, while a CCPC that is a Qualifying Corporation receives 40% refundability on its 15% ITCs earned above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, an ECPC earns 0% refundability above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit.

body.text: 3.4 Section 37 Deductible Pool, Carrybacks, Carryforwards, and Next-Year Taxability

Allowable current and post-December 15, 2024 capital SR&ED expenditures performed in Canada enter the claimant's Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures and may be fully deducted against business income in the taxation year incurred. Where a claimant deducts an SR&ED capital expenditure from the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(b), that deduction is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance, and the asset must not be entered on T2 Schedule 8.

For non-refundable SR&ED ITC balances, subsection 127(5) provides a 3-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward to offset Part I federal income tax payable. Under CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, an ITC carryback to any of the three preceding taxation years is capped at the lesser of: (1) the current year's available ITC exceeding what was required to reduce current-year Part I tax to nil, and (2) the target prior year's Part I tax otherwise payable in excess of ITCs already available in that prior year. Any ITC refunded in cash is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax in that year, removing it from carryback or carryforward balances. Where a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control, statutory restrictions limit both the carryforward of pre-acquisition ITCs and the carryback of post-acquisition ITCs, whereas a statutory amalgamation under section 87 deems the new corporation to be a continuation of each predecessor corporation for section 37 pool purposes.

Crucially, federal SR&ED ITCs deducted against tax or refunded in cash are included in taxable income in the following taxation year (via reduction of the Section 37 pool or, for Shared-Use-Equipment ITCs, reduction of the subsequent year's CCA class undepreciated capital cost). By contrast, provincial R&D tax credits and government grants reduce federal qualified SR&ED expenditures as government assistance in the current taxation year.
4. Qualifying Expenditures and Overhead Methodologies
4.1 Salaries, Wages, Specified Employees, and 2025–2027 YMPE Ceilings

Employee salaries and wages qualify for SR&ED to the extent employees are directly engaged in SR&ED—defined in CRA's Glossary and Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated March 27, 2026) as hands-on technical work determined strictly by the actual tasks performed, never by an employee's job title. Where employees perform permissible SR&ED work outside Canada that qualifies to be deemed incurred in Canada, those wages enter the SR&ED salary base subject to the specific foreign-salary limits set out in Section 10.0 of CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy.

CRA rules sharply distinguish non-specified employees from specified employees. For non-specified employees, the Traditional Method allows directly engaged wages paid in the year (or within 180 days of year-end), including bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year. Under the Proxy Method, while regular directly engaged salaries qualify for the Section 37 pool, the salary base for calculating the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR excludes bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, employer-paid related benefit contributions, and prior-year unpaid amounts paid in the year (reported separately on Line 310 of Form T661).

For specified employees, bonuses and remuneration based on profits are completely excluded under both the Traditional and Proxy methods. In addition, specified employee salaries are subject to statutory ceilings tied to the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE)—specifically the first earnings ceiling under the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), not the higher CPP2 second earnings ceiling ($73,200 in 2024, $81,200 in 2025, and $85,000 in 2026). Under the Traditional Method (and for overall SR&ED salary eligibility), a specified employee's claimable SR&ED wages (including taxable benefits and prior paid amounts under Traditional) are capped at 5 times the YMPE (5 × YMPE). Under the Proxy Method (subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the ITR), the maximum salary included in the PPA salary base for a specified employee is the lesser of: (1) total eligible salary (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages) multiplied by the percentage of time spent on SR&ED, capped at 75%, and (2) 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365), where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the tax year ends and B is the number of days in the tax year the claimant employed the individual. If a specified employee is employed by associated corporations (including deemed associations with related individuals or partnerships) with tax years ending in the same calendar year, the 2.5 × YMPE ceiling must be shared across the associated group.

body.text: 4.2 Overhead Calculation: Prescribed Proxy Amount (55%) vs. Traditional Method

Claimants must elect annually on Form T661 between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method for SR&ED overhead. Under the Proxy Method, actual SR&ED overhead expenditures cannot be claimed as SR&ED expenditures; instead, the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible salary base under subsection 2900(4) of the ITR. The PPA is used solely to calculate qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes—it is not added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and is not deducted as an SR&ED expense, because the underlying actual overhead expenses remain deductible as ordinary business expenses. In low-overhead corporate structures, the PPA is further constrained by an Overall Cap equal to A − B − C, where A is total business deductions claimed in calculating net income for tax purposes (including cost of goods sold), B is deductions claimed under sections 20 (such as CCA, interest, and bad debts), 24, 26, 30, 32, 37 (SR&ED pool deductions), 66 to 66.8, and 104 of the ITA, and C is expenditures incurred for the use of, or right to use, a building.

Under the Traditional Method, no notional PPA is calculated. Instead, the claimant itemizes actual overhead and other expenditures (reported on Line 360 of Form T661) that are both directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada and incremental (meaning they would not have been incurred if the SR&ED premises, facilities, equipment, or activities had not existed). Examples include maintenance and upkeep of dedicated SR&ED facilities or equipment, incremental retiring allowances, and—for lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024—the SR&ED portion of lease payments on equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time.

body.text: 4.3 Materials Consumed and Transformed, Custom Components, and ITC Recapture

Under CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy and Glossary, eligible direct materials comprise materials consumed (materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of SR&ED testing) and materials transformed into prototypes, custom products, commercial assets, or experimental production runs. However, under subsections 127(27), 127(28), 127(29), and 127(32) of the ITA and CRA's Recapture of Investment Tax Credit Policy, selling or converting SR&ED property to commercial use triggers SR&ED ITC recapture (as well as potential CCA recapture reported on Line 440 of Form T661). Property subject to ITC recapture includes materials incorporated into a custom product, commercial asset, or production run, ≥90% ASA equipment, Shared-Use-Equipment, experimental animals and plants, and property acquired under an SR&ED contract.

CRA policy underscores a major structural difference in recapture cost between outsourced component fabrication and in-house fabrication. In Section 7.1.1 of the Recapture of Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant pays an arm's-length supplier $12,000 to manufacture and develop an SR&ED component ($10,000 manufacturing/development cost plus $2,000 supplier profit) and later converts or sells that property commercially, the entire $12,000 purchase cost is subject to ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) and 127(32). If that exact same part is manufactured in-house by the claimant, there is no ITC recapture on the internal salaries or overhead expended to build the part—only the underlying material cost is exposed to recapture.
4.4 Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, Taxable Suppliers, 180-Day Unpaid Amounts, and Non-Arm's-Length Rules

Under CRA's Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy (updated May 22, 2026), external R&D contracts, institutional payments, and related-party transactions are governed by strict statutory adjustments.

Where a claimant contracts with an arm's-length entity to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada, or makes an eligible third-party payment for SR&ED (such as to a Canadian university), only 80% of the expenditure qualifies for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9) (qualified expenditure paragraph (a)(ii)), with the remaining 20% deducted on Form T661. Offshore work performed outside Canada does not qualify. Moreover, under the Taxable Supplier Rules, a current SR&ED contract expenditure paid or payable to (or for the benefit of) a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier is completely excluded from qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. A "taxable supplier" means a person resident in Canada, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident person or non-Canadian partnership receiving the amount in the course of carrying on a business through a permanent establishment in Canada. Conducting physical R&D inside Canada is insufficient if the non-resident contractor lacks a Canadian permanent establishment; this prevents foreign-conduit double-dipping by two Canadian companies on the same R&D work. However, the taxable supplier exclusion does not apply to current expenditures where the SR&ED is directly undertaken by the claimant itself.

Under subsection 127(26), any current SR&ED expenditure (whether salary, contract, or overhead) that remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which it was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that tax year for ITC purposes. For an unpaid arm's-length contract, 100% of the unpaid expenditure is excluded from earning ITCs in the year incurred (reported as a 20% contract reduction plus an 80% unpaid current expenditure reduction on Form T661), and when subsequently paid in a later taxation year, only 80% of the amount paid is added back on the "payment of prior years' unpaid amounts" line.

When a claimant contracts for SR&ED with a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer, the payer's contract outlay is excluded from qualified expenditures. Instead, the NAL performer may transfer its qualified SR&ED expenditures to the NAL payer using Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026). The transferable amount is capped at the least of three figures: (1) the amount specified on Form T1146, (2) the performer's pre-transfer SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at year-end, and (3) total amounts paid by the payer within 180 days of the performer's year-end that would qualify as arm's-length contract payments for paid NAL qualified expenditures (or amounts transferred from another NAL party). Audit teams must watch three severe statutory traps here: first, if a performer attempts to transfer more than its pre-transfer qualified expenditure pool, the Income Tax Act dictates that no amount ($0) can be transferred; second, partnerships cannot transfer or receive NAL qualified expenditures because a partnership is not a "person" under these rules; and third, if the payer's tax year-end precedes the performer's tax year-end, the payer's ITC claim is deferred until its first tax year ending at or after the performer's transfer year. Finally, when purchasing goods, services, or post-December 15, 2024 equipment leases (deemed to be services) from a NAL supplier, Lines 542 and 543 of Form T661 cap the qualified amount at the lesser of the claimant's cost or the supplier's traced adjusted selling cost (A − B) or adjusted service cost (A − B − C − D − E), and property originally received by a NAL supplier as a gift has a deemed adjusted selling cost of nil.
4.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Cloud/Compute Infrastructure, Leases, and Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE)

Under Bill C-15 and CRA's revised SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), and SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), capital property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, are once again eligible for SR&ED deductions and ITCs. Practitioner analyses from KPMG and SRJ Chartered Professional Accountants note that this restoration brings R&D laboratory and testing instruments, prototyping machinery, specialized tools, AI/ML GPU and compute infrastructure, and eligible software and development cloud space fees into play alongside traditional hardware. To claim capital property under CRA's ownership rules (paragraph 20(1)(a), paragraph 37(1)(b), and subsection 13(21)), the claimant must acquire ownership or a leasehold interest in depreciable property (not merely construct an unowned structure on another party's land or hold property as an agent/nominee). Land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are strictly ineligible.
Qualifying depreciable equipment falls into one of two statutory tracks based on SR&ED usage intensity:

Under the Full SR&ED Capital Expenditure Track (All or Substantially All — ASA ≥90%), property reported on Line 390 (deductible pool) and Line 535 (ITC base) of Form T661 must be intended at acquisition either to be used 90% or more of its operating time over its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to have 90% or more of its value consumed in performing SR&ED in Canada. Capital cost includes purchase price, installation, customs and excise duties, transportation, and direct acquisition costs, excluding borrowing/interest charges. A critical audit distinction separates new versus used equipment: used equipment (such as equipment used regularly for commercial demonstration, though prospective-purchaser testing normally does not taint new status, and refurbished equipment may qualify in certain cases) enters the Section 37 deductible pool on Line 390 but is a prescribed expenditure under ITR paragraph 2902(b) and earns $0 in SR&ED ITCs. (For leased new property, a lessor and first lessee may jointly elect to deem the property directly acquired by the lessee so it is not treated as previously used or leased.) General-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) is excluded under the Proxy Method. Claimants must list their 20 most expensive ASA capital properties in Part 6B of Form T661 and omit Line 390 assets from T2 Schedule 8.

Under the Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) Track (subsection 127(9), Line 504 and Part 6C / Box 792 of Form T661), new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the ≥90% ASA test—and is neither Prescribed Depreciable Property (buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, or property intended at acquisition to be used/consumed primarily in non-SR&ED over its useful life) nor GPOEF (excluded under both Proxy and Traditional methods)—can earn partial ITCs across two periods. If the equipment is used primarily for SR&ED in Canada during its operating time in the first period—running from the available-for-use date to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that date—25% (one-quarter) of its capital cost qualifies for the ITC as first-term SUE. If it was claimed as first-term SUE and is again used primarily for SR&ED during the second period (ending at the close of the following taxation year), another 25% of its capital cost qualifies as second-term SUE. For example, in CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, a $300,000 machine available for use on January 2, 2025, by a calendar-year company and used 81% (2,900 of 3,600 operating hours) in SR&ED earns a $75,000 (25%) qualified expenditure in the tax year ending December 31, 2026 (first period ≥12 months), and a second $75,000 (25%) qualified expenditure in the tax year ending December 31, 2027. SUE capital cost does not enter the Section 37 pool; it is depreciated on T2 Schedule 8, any SUE ITC claimed/refunded reduces next year's CCA class UCC, excess government assistance on Term 1 carries forward to reduce Term 2, NAL SUE purchases apply adjusted selling cost directly on Line 504 (not Line 543), and the 20 most expensive SUE assets must be itemized in Part 6C.

body.text: 5. Administration, Filing Deadlines, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Defence
5.1 Governing Authorities, 2026 Updated Forms, and the Strict 18-Month Statutory Bar

Tax policy design for SR&ED rests with the Department of Finance Canada, while nationwide claim processing, technical/financial review, and harmonized provincial credit administration are carried out by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Non-tax innovation grants and IP support programs that stack with SR&ED are administered separately by the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED).

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the "investment tax credit" definition in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, prescribed forms (Form T661 and T2 Schedule 31 for corporate claimants) must be filed within 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the SR&ED expenditures were incurred. For a corporation with a December 31, 2024 year-end, the absolute statutory deadline was June 30, 2026; for a December 31, 2025 year-end, it is June 30, 2027. There is no administrative extension mechanism—missing the 18-month deadline forfeits both Section 37 deductibility and ITC entitlement permanently. Most corporate claimants aim to file Form T661 with their T2 return within six months of fiscal year-end so cash refunds are processed promptly and any technical clarifications can be addressed well inside the 18-month window. (Practitioners at Scitax noted during spring 2026 that commercial tax software suites such as Wolters Kluwer Taxprep faced short-term release lags awaiting May 2026 form updates following Bill C-15's March 26, 2026 Royal Assent.)

body.text: 5.2 Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional, free Pre-Claim Approval Process via My Business Account. Designed to give businesses upfront certainty before commencing R&D or incurring project costs (or right as a project begins), the process delivers a formal CRA project eligibility determination within eight weeks. Per CRA's How to apply for pre-claim approval guidelines, an applicant is eligible to apply if it is a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a partnership, has gross business income under $25,000,000, and is in good standing with the CRA.

For claims that complete pre-claim approval and subsequently require a post-filing expenditure review, CRA processing time is cut in half from 180 days to 90 days. Claimants may also request one-on-one CRA pre-claim outreach consultations (OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca) or attend monthly CRA Microsoft Teams informational webinars.
5.3 CRA Reviews, Contemporaneous Documentation, Penalties, and Dispute Resolution

In the most recent reporting year, CRA data indicates that 90% of SR&ED claims were accepted as filed, 6% were accepted with modifications, and 4% were denied. Note also that in 2026 the CRA permanently archived its Guidelines for SR&ED claims made by physicians and medical professional corporations – Information for claimants, directing medical corporations to general SR&ED policies.

Under CRA administrative guidance (The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants and Gross Negligence Penalty on SR&ED Claims), audit defence rests on contemporaneous project records created during the R&D (rather than reconstructed after the fact), readiness for CRA technical interviews and expenditure verification, avoidance of civil gross-negligence penalties on overstated claims, and—where a claim is reduced or disallowed—requesting a local-office second-level review, filing a formal Notice of Objection (for which Budget 2026 proposed extending the statutory filing timeframe), and appealing to the Tax Court of Canada.
Corporate tax teams preparing claims under the 2026 rules should implement six sequential compliance controls:

items: Submit Pre-Claim Approval Applications for New Projects: Where gross business income is under $25 million, apply via My Business Account before incurring project costs to secure an eight-week eligibility ruling and 90-day post-filing expenditure review service standard.

Capture Contemporaneous Technical and Project-Tagged Records: Record hypotheses, test iterations, code commits, benchmark runs, and timesheets as work occurs, and—anticipating Budget 2026's enactment for tax years starting on or after November 5, 2026—tag initial regulatory validation studies and IP registration/maintenance invoices to discrete SR&ED project IDs separate from general overhead.

Maintain Post-December 15, 2024 Capital and Operating-Time Logs: Document purchase invoices, available-for-use dates, "new" provenance, and operating-hour logs to substantiate ≥90% ASA equipment (Line 390 / Part 6B) versus Shared-Use-Equipment (Line 504 / Part 6C).

Enforce 180-Day Payment Clearance and NAL Transfer Audits: Settle all accrued SR&ED wages and contractor invoices within 180 days of year-end under subsection 127(26), verify Canadian permanent establishment status for non-resident contractors, and confirm Form T1146 transfers never exceed the performer's pre-transfer qualified pool.

Optimize Phase-Out Elections and Schedule 49 Allocations: For CCPCs with prior-year taxable capital above $15 million, compare the default taxable capital phase-out against the elective three-year average gross revenue test, and file Schedule 49 across all associated corporations.

Lock Filing Calendars Ahead of the 18-Month Statutory Gate: File Form T661 and T2 Schedule 31 alongside the six-month T2 corporate return and enforce a strict internal cut-off well ahead of the non-extendable 18-month statutory deadline.

body.text: 6. Provincial R&D Tax Incentives and Non-Dilutive Grant Stacking
6.1 Québec's Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) and AI Credits

Québec fundamentally restructured its provincial R&D tax landscape in its 2025–2026 Budget (Information Bulletin 2025-6), replacing eight legacy provincial R&D tax credits (including the former 14%–30% R&D salary tax credit) with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation, Codes 112 and 113). Effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, CRIC is available to any corporation (CCPC, public corporation, or foreign-owned subsidiary of any size) operating a business with an establishment in Québec.

Under Gouvernement du Québec and Revenu Québec guidelines, CRIC provides a 30% refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above an annual exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable tax credit on all qualified expenditures exceeding $1,000,000 (with associated corporations allocating the $1,000,000 bracket on Form RD-1029.8.EN-T). Crucially, CRIC covers both Québec R&D and pre-commercialization activities (such as regulatory compliance testing and product design carried out in conjunction with Québec R&D, reported with Form RD-1029.8.PR-T). Qualified CRIC expenditures comprise 100% of Québec employee R&D/pre-commercialization salaries, 100% of eligible capital property acquisition costs (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land/buildings—earning 100% refundability rather than the federal 40% cap), 50% of payments to Québec subcontractors, and 50% of payments to eligible public research centres, research consortia, or university entities. Before the 30%/20% rates apply, total qualified expenditures must exceed an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec personal income tax basic personal amount (cited in practitioner guides at $18,571–$18,751 per full-time equivalent in 2025) prorated by each employee's time on eligible activities.

Claimants file Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (2026-09 version) with their CO-17 return within 18 months of fiscal year-end. The same dollar of expenditure cannot be combined under CRIC and another Québec credit—such as the C3i credit, the CDTIM multimedia title credit (up to 37.5%), or Québec's new CDAEIA 30% refundable AI adoption salary credit (effective for fiscal years beginning in 2026 to replace the legacy CDAE e-business credit, requiring Investissement Québec attestation within 15–18 months of year-end).
6.2 Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), Ontario Misalignment, and Other Provinces

Across the rest of Canada, provincial R&D tax credits stack onto federal SR&ED either via separate provincial administration in Ontario, Québec, and Alberta, or via CRA-administered T2 schedules in British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland and Labrador (while Prince Edward Island and the territories have no separate provincial/territorial R&D credits).

Critically, provincial caps and phase-out ranges in Ontario and Alberta did not move when federal Bill C-15 enacted the $6 million limit and $15 million–$75 million phase-out. In Alberta, practitioner and grant summaries confirm that the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)—claimed on Schedule 29 of the Alberta AT1 return for federal-matching SR&ED expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020—provides an 8% refundable credit and up to 20% up to a $4,000,000 annual expenditure limit, but still phases out over $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 of taxable capital (reaching $0 at $50,000,000). Similarly, in Ontario, practitioner guidance highlights that the refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) expenditure limit remains $3,000,000, half the new $6,000,000 federal limit.

body.text: 6.3 Grant Integration (NRC IRAP, Technoclimat, Elevate IP) and Stacking Calculation

Direct cost-shared innovation grants—such as NRC IRAP (negotiated upfront prior to spending), ISED Elevate IP and NRC IP Assist, Québec Technoclimat ($100,000–$18 million cleantech grants, capped at 75% combined government support) and Programme Innovation — Primo-Adoptants ($10,000–$75,000), or Alberta Innovates AICE (up to $300,000–$600,000 covering up to 75% of eligible costs)—stack with SR&ED as government assistance. Under CRA's Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, provincial R&D tax credits and direct grants received or receivable by the filing-due date reduce federal qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar (while subsequent repayments of assistance are added back in the year repaid). However, under the federal Proxy Method, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount is calculated on the eligible salary base before subtracting government assistance—preserving the full notional overhead credit. (Note per CRA policy that rules for reducing the Section 37 deductible pool for assistance differ from those for the ITC qualified pool and are governed by CRA's separate Assistance and Contract Payments Policy.)
